Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented four-manifold without boundary. Its smooth
structure is retained throughout. A **classical finite-regularity
trivial-potential configuration** consists of a time-oriented $C^3$
Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, a global real $C^2$ one-form
$A$, and a global complex $C^2$ scalar $\varphi$. Fix
$c,G_N,\mu_0,K_\varphi>0$, $\lambda,\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and
$V\in C^\infty(\mathcal U;\mathbb R)$ for an open
$\mathcal U\subset\mathbb R$ containing $|\varphi|^2(M)$. Set
$\kappa_E=8\pi G_N/c^4$. The curvature sign, length-coordinate convention
$x^0=ct$, and SI assignments are those of
[[def-emg-trivial-potential-charged-scalar-system]]; only these formulas and
conventions are imported, not that item's smooth-field restriction.

The Levi-Civita connection and curvature here are defined by their coordinate
formulas for this $C^3$ metric. Define

$$F_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a,\qquad P_a:=\mathcal D_a\varphi:=\partial_a\varphi-i\lambda A_a\varphi,$$

$$\mathcal D_aP_b:=\nabla_aP_b-i\lambda A_aP_b,\qquad E_\varphi:=g^{ab}\mathcal D_aP_b-V'(|\varphi|^2)\varphi,$$

$$L_\varphi:=g^{ab}\overline{P_a}P_b+V(|\varphi|^2),\qquad j^a:=K_\varphi\lambda\operatorname{Im}(\overline\varphi P^a),$$

$$T^\varphi_{ab}:=K_\varphi\operatorname{Re}(\overline{P_a}P_b)-\frac{K_\varphi}{2}g_{ab}L_\varphi,\qquad T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}\left(F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right).$$

Conjugate charged derivatives use the opposite gauge sign. All indices are
raised with $g^{-1}$. Thus $F,P$ are $C^1$, $j,T^\varphi,T^{\mathrm{EM}}$
are $C^1$, $E_\varphi$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}$ are continuous, and the
Einstein tensor $G$ is $C^1$. The **classical charged-scalar equations** are
the pointwise equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b,\qquad E_\varphi=0,\qquad G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa_E(T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}+T^\varphi_{ab}).$$

Here $dF=0$ already follows from $F=dA$ with $A\in C^2$. These are equations
for the declared classical fields; they do not assert existence, smoothness
improvement, or a weaker distributional theory.

For a continuous compactly supported real top form $\omega$, define
$\mathcal I_M(\omega)$ by a finite smooth cutoff localization near its
support and the signed Riemann integrals of the resulting chart
coefficients, extended by zero. The construction and its independence are
proved below. For a complex top form extend $\mathcal I_M$ by integrating
its real and imaginary parts separately. For a configuration
$X=(g,A,\varphi)$ put

$$\mathscr L(X):=\left[\frac{c^3}{16\pi G_N}(R(g)-2\Lambda)-\frac{1}{4\mu_0c}F_{ab}F^{ab}-\frac{K_\varphi}{2c}L_\varphi\right]\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

If $X_1=X_0$ outside a compact set, its **relative total action** is
$S(X_1;X_0):=\mathcal I_M(\mathscr L(X_1)-\mathscr L(X_0))$. The scalar
and Maxwell relative actions are defined by their respective summands. No
subtraction of divergent global integrals is intended. When the separate
global integrals are defined and finite, this agrees with their difference.

Allowed independent directions are smooth compactly supported symmetric
inverse-metric tensors $q^{ab}$, real one-forms $\alpha$, and complex scalars
$\eta$. Near zero parameter use

$$g_\varepsilon^{-1}=g^{-1}+\varepsilon q,\qquad A_\varepsilon=A+\varepsilon\alpha,\qquad\varphi_\varepsilon=\varphi+\varepsilon\eta.$$

The parameter interval is restricted to preserve signature, time orientation,
and the potential domain. Stationarity means that the derivative of the
relative total action vanishes for every such direction. These definitions
include the original smooth trivial-potential system as a subclass, with its
same action coefficients and tensors. They do not change the separate
nontrivial-circle-bundle formulation or impose an integer condition on the
real coupling $\lambda$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Since $\varphi\equiv0$, every derivative of $\varphi$ is zero and $P_a=\mathcal D_a\varphi=0$. Hence $E_\varphi=\mathcal D_aP^a-V'(0)\varphi=0$ and $j^a=K_\varphi\lambda\operatorname{Im}(\overline\varphi P^a)=0$. Also $g^{ab}\overline{P_a}P_b+V(|\varphi|^2)=V(0)=0$, so the defining formula gives $T^\varphi_{ab}=0$.

Substitution of $j=0$ and $T^\varphi=0$ into [F1] leaves exactly $\nabla_aF^{ab}=0$, $dF=0$, and $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa_E T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}$, the displayed assumptions. Thus the zero extension solves the full classical model. For compatible zero-scalar Cauchy data, [L1] supplies a local development. In its temporal gauge, $\partial_0=n$ initially, so $\pi_0=\pi_n=0$ there; the charged spatial compatibility gives $\pi_i=\mathcal D_i\varphi_0=0$ as well. Hence the real scalar state $z=(\operatorname{Re}\varphi,\operatorname{Im}\varphi, \operatorname{Re}\pi_0,\operatorname{Im}\pi_0, \operatorname{Re}\pi_i,\operatorname{Im}\pi_i)$ has zero initial data.

In the admissible coordinates, the scalar first-order equations have
$\partial_0\varphi=\pi_0$ and the $\pi$-block
$$A^0_\pi\partial_0\pi+\sum_kA^k_\pi\partial_k\pi+\text{zero-order terms}=0,$$
where
$$A^0_\pi=\begin{pmatrix}-g^{00}&0\\0&(g^{ij})\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^k_\pi=\begin{pmatrix}-2g^{0k}&-g^{kj}\\-g^{ik}&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
These are real symmetric matrices, with $A^0_\pi$ positive definite because
$g^{00}<0$ and $(g^{ij})$ is positive definite. Adding the scalar transport
equation gives symmetric matrices $A^0=I\oplus A^0_\pi$ and
$A^k=0\oplus A^k_\pi$ on the real state $z$, so the full scalar system is
$A^0\partial_0z+\sum_kA^k\partial_kz+C_0z=0$. The remaining terms can be
written $C_0z$ with $C_0$ bounded on each compact solution cylinder: they are
linear in $\varphi,\pi_0,\pi_i$, with coefficients formed from $\Gamma(g)$,
$A_i$, $F_{0i}$ and $V'(|\varphi|^2)$. The metric and matter regularity in
[L1] gives $g\in C^3$ and $A,\varphi\in C^2$ in the finite-Sobolev branch
at $s\ge5$; hence $A^0,A^k$ are continuously differentiable and $C_0$ is
continuous there.
Writing $e=z^{\mathsf T}A^0z$ and $f^k=z^{\mathsf T}A^kz$, symmetry and the
system equation give
$$\partial_0e+\sum_k\partial_kf^k=z^{\mathsf T}\left(\partial_0A^0+\sum_k\partial_kA^k-C_0-C_0^{\mathsf T}\right)z.$$
The matrix on the right is bounded, while $A^0\ge aI$ for some $a>0$ on
the compact cylinder. On the periodic torus, integrating this identity gives
$E'\le CE$ for $E=\int e$, since the spatial fluxes cancel at opposite
periodic faces. In a local chart, choose a coordinate cube $Q_0$ around the
initial point and shrink each side at a speed $\sigma$ satisfying
$\sigma a>\max_k\sup\|A^k\|$. Differentiating the integral over the moving
cube and integrating each spatial derivative by the one-variable fundamental
theorem of calculus gives
$$E'(t)\le CE(t)-\sum_{\text{faces }S}\int_S z^{\mathsf T}(\sigma A^0+\nu_kA^k)z\,dS\le CE(t),$$
where $\nu=\pm\partial_k$ is the outward coordinate normal on each face; the
face matrices are positive definite by the choice of $\sigma$. In either
domain $E(0)=0$ and $E\ge0$, so integrating the inequality and applying [F2]
gives $E=0$ forward and backward in time. Positivity of $A^0$ and continuity
of $z$ then give $\varphi=\pi=0$ near every initial point. This proves the
zero branch for finite-Sobolev data without using smooth geometric uniqueness;
for smooth data, [L1] additionally identifies the branch up to its stated
isometry and gauge.
